translationRepairs: King Wu had ten brothers from the same mother.
King Wu was one of ten brothers born to the same mother.
The count of ten includes King Wu himself. The revision states that relationship directly and avoids the proposal's awkward compound 'same-mother brothers.'
Therefore, enfeoffed Shu Xian at Guan, enfeoffed Shu Du at Cai: two people assisted Zhou son Wu Geng Lu Fu, governed Yin remnant people.
He therefore enfeoffed Shu Xian at Guan and Shu Du at Cai. The two men assisted Wu Geng Lufu, son of King Zhou of Shang, in governing the remnant people of Yin.
紂 is King Zhou of Shang and modifies 子, making Wu Geng Lufu his son. The revision restores the omitted subject and removes the proposal's ambiguous 'Zhou of Shang.'
The other son, Kang Shu, was enfeoffed as lord of Wei and became known as Kang Shu of Wei.
Over the other group he enfeoffed Kang Shu as lord of Wei, thereafter known as Kang Shu of Wei.
其一 resumes the division of the Yin remnants into two groups in the preceding sentence. It does not call Kang Shu 'the other son.'
In the twenty-ninth year, Duke Mu died, and his son Duke Zhuang succeeded on the jiawu day.
In the twenty-ninth year, Duke Mu died, and his son Jiawu, Duke Zhuang, succeeded him.
甲午 is the ruler's given name Jiawu, not a sexagenary date. The apposition distinguishes his personal name from his posthumous title.
In the twenty-ninth year, Duke Mu died, and his son Duke Zhuang succeeded on jiawu.
In the twenty-ninth year, Duke Mu died, and his son Jiawu, Duke Zhuang, succeeded him.
The literal field also misreads 甲午 as a date. It is the personal name Jiawu attached to Duke Zhuang in the standard succession formula.
The proposed wording accurately supplies the possessive article and renders 亡去 simply as 'fled.'
